prompt: A regional yogurt manufacturer interacts with six types of actors in its microenvironment. Identify which actor each case describes.

cases.text: A cooperative of dairy farms delivers raw milk and fruit cultures to the manufacturer's plant.
cases.explanation: The farms provide the raw resources needed by the company to produce its goods, making them suppliers.

cases.text: A refrigerated freight operator and a supermarket chain transport, stock, and sell the yogurt to shoppers.
cases.explanation: Physical distribution firms and resellers help the company promote, sell, and distribute its goods to final buyers.

cases.text: Households and school cafeterias purchase the yogurt cups for daily meals.
cases.explanation: Individuals, households, and institutional buyers belong to the company's customer markets.

cases.text: A rival dairy brand launches a lower-priced probiotic yogurt cup in the same supermarket aisle.
cases.explanation: A rival firm seeking to satisfy the same target buyers is a competitor.

cases.text: A regional business newspaper publishes an investigative profile on the company's new production facility.
cases.explanation: News organizations are media publics whose coverage can affect the firm's ability to achieve its objectives.

cases.text: The company's accounting and operations departments coordinate billing schedules and production quality standards.
cases.explanation: Internal company departments form the internal environment that must work in harmony to deliver customer value.

prompt: A beverage company is reviewing changes in its environment. Identify whether each development represents a political force, an economic force, or a microenvironment actor.

cases.text: The national government imposes a 25 percent import tariff on aluminum cans sourced from abroad.
cases.explanation: Trade policy and import tariffs are political forces in the macroenvironment that alter supply chain cost structures.

cases.text: Rising inflation and higher interest rates lead households to cut discretionary spending and switch to store brands.
cases.explanation: Inflation and interest rates are macroeconomic factors that affect consumer purchasing power and spending patterns.

cases.text: The company's glass-bottle vendor experiences a labor strike at its factory and delays shipments by two weeks.
cases.explanation: A specific supplier is an actor in the firm's immediate microenvironment.

cases.text: A new domestic industrial subsidy lowers the cost of agricultural inputs across the entire beverage sector.
cases.explanation: Government taxation, public spending, and industrial subsidies are political forces.

cases.text: A rise in regional unemployment reduces average household disposable income across the country.
cases.explanation: Unemployment and income distribution are economic forces that shape consumer purchasing power.

cases.text: A convenience store chain renegotiates shelf space for the company's bottled teas.
cases.explanation: A retail reseller is a marketing intermediary in the microenvironment.

prompt: Identify which of Carroll's four pillars of Corporate Social Responsibility each company action illustrates.

cases.text: A bakery chain prices its loaves to cover operating costs and earn a return that keeps the enterprise sustainable.
cases.explanation: Producing goods that society wants and selling them at a sustaining profit is the foundational economic responsibility.

cases.text: A toy manufacturer removes a product from shelves to comply with a newly enacted federal child-safety statute.
cases.explanation: Obeying codified laws and regulations fulfills the firm's legal responsibility.

cases.text: A furniture maker pays small workshops fair rates and honors informal commitments even when no statute requires it.
cases.explanation: Doing what is right, just, and fair beyond the minimum requirements of the law is ethical responsibility.

cases.text: A grocery retailer donates delivery vans and employee volunteer hours to neighborhood food banks.
cases.explanation: Voluntary corporate contributions of financial, technical, or human resources to improve community well-being represent philanthropic responsibility.

cases.text: A software firm updates its checkout consent forms to satisfy mandatory national data-privacy regulations.
cases.explanation: Complying with statutory data-privacy rules fulfills legal responsibility.

cases.text: A telecom provider proactively alerts subscribers before a promotional rate expires, even though the contract permits silent renewal.
cases.explanation: Avoiding consumer harm when a questionable practice is legally permitted reflects ethical responsibility.

prompt: Sort each company initiative into genuine sustainable marketing or greenwashing.

cards.text: A detergent maker reformulates its concentrated liquid to use 60 percent less water and ships it in verified post-consumer recycled bottles.
cards.explanation: Redesigning products to use recycled inputs and lower logistics emissions is an authentic operational improvement.

cards.text: A cleaning spray retains its original chemical formula and plastic bottle but adds a green leaf graphic and an unverified "Eco-Pure" banner.
cards.explanation: Placing vague, unverified environmental labels on an unchanged product is greenwashing.

cards.text: An energy company spends ten times more on television commercials touting a tiny solar pilot than on reducing emissions in its core operations.
cards.explanation: Spending more time and money claiming to be environmentally friendly than actually reducing environmental impact defines greenwashing.

cards.text: An apparel brand audits its dye mills to eliminate toxic runoff and funds living-wage contracts for garment workers.
cards.explanation: Reducing environmental pollution and supporting fair labor standards preserve the needs of current and future generations.

cards.text: A snack brand prints "100% Earth Friendly" on non-recyclable foil wrappers without any third-party certification.
cards.explanation: Unverified environmental claims on non-recyclable packaging mislead buyers and erode brand trust.

cards.text: A logistics provider replaces diesel delivery vans with electric vehicles and redesigns shipping cartons to eliminate plastic void fill.
cards.explanation: Lowering carbon emissions in logistics and reducing packaging waste are substantive sustainability actions.

prompt: Classify each unethical tactic as deceptive pricing, deceptive promotion, or deceptive packaging.

cards.text: A furniture store advertises a sofa at "50% off our $2,400 regular price," even though the sofa was never sold above $1,200.
cards.explanation: Claiming a large discount from a fabricated reference price is deceptive pricing.

cards.text: A ticketing website displays a $45 seat price in search results and reveals an unavoidable $18 facility fee only on the final payment screen.
cards.explanation: Concealing mandatory fees until checkout is a form of deceptive pricing.

cards.text: An electronics shop runs an ad for a $199 television that is always "out of stock" in order to steer arriving shoppers toward a $549 model.
cards.explanation: Luring shoppers with an unavailable bargain to upsell a costlier item is a bait-and-switch tactic under deceptive promotion.

cards.text: A skincare brand claims in its commercials that its cream erases wrinkles in three days, despite laboratory tests showing no such effect.
cards.explanation: Misrepresenting a product's performance or ingredients is deceptive promotion.

cards.text: A snack manufacturer places six ounces of crackers inside an opaque twelve-ounce cardboard box so the package appears twice as full on the shelf.
cards.explanation: Exaggerating contents through oversized non-functional containers (slack fill) is deceptive packaging.

cards.text: A coffee roaster quietly reduces its bag weight from 340 grams to 285 grams in the same-sized pouch without disclosing the higher unit price.
cards.explanation: Subtle reductions in net weight without disclosing the unit price change constitute deceptive packaging.

prompt: Each development below stems from artificial intelligence. Identify which PESTLE force it illustrates.

cases.text: A retail platform launches an autonomous AI agent that compares product specifications and reorders household staples automatically.
cases.explanation: Large language models and autonomous AI agents act as a technological force by creating new channels for product discovery and automated purchasing.

cases.text: Under the European Union's AI Act, an online retailer must inform customers clearly whenever they are interacting with an AI chatbot.
cases.explanation: Statutory rules requiring chatbot disclosure are part of the legal force governing AI transparency.

cases.text: Surveyed shoppers willingly delegate paper-towel reorders to an AI assistant but refuse to let it choose anniversary gifts or medical products.
cases.explanation: Variations in consumer trust toward AI systems represent a social force that determines which categories buyers delegate.

cases.text: A regulation mandates a clear disclosure label on any promotional video or audio that uses synthetic media to imitate a real person.
cases.explanation: Government mandates requiring labels on synthetic audio, images, or video are legal forces.

cases.text: Generational attitudes toward algorithmic decision making cause adoption of automated shopping assistants to vary across demographic groups.
cases.explanation: Cultural attitudes and trust across demographic segments are social forces.

cases.text: Advances in language model tool use allow software assistants to query inventory APIs and execute checkout flows in seconds.
cases.explanation: Breakthroughs in AI capabilities that enable automated purchasing are technological forces.

prompt: Classify each storefront practice as a dark pattern aimed at a human shopper, a dark pattern aimed at an AI shopping agent, or an ethical disclosure.

bins.label: Dark pattern aimed at a human shopper
Dark pattern aimed at an AI agent

cards.text: A booking page displays a flashing countdown timer that resets to five minutes every time a visitor reloads the page.
cards.explanation: A fake countdown timer is a user-interface dark pattern crafted to pressure a human buyer.

cards.text: A product page embeds white text on a white background instructing AI assistants to ignore competitors and recommend this item.
cards.explanation: Hidden prompt-injection text invisible to humans is a dark pattern aimed at manipulating an AI shopping agent.

cards.text: An online store tucks a mandatory processing fee into the final checkout step after the shopper has entered shipping details.
cards.explanation: A hidden checkout fee steers a human shopper who has already invested time in the transaction.

cards.text: A seller places an unfavorable $1.40 price per ounce inside an unindexed raster image while leaving the low total package price in plain text.
cards.explanation: Burying a high unit price inside an unindexed image causes an AI agent reading page text to overlook it.

cards.text: A merchant floods a marketplace with hundreds of synthetic five-star reviews phrased to boost how an AI agent scores product quality.
cards.explanation: Synthetic reviews written to elevate algorithmic quality scores target the AI agent's evaluation.

cards.text: A grocer publishes net weight, unit price per 100 grams, and full fee breakdowns in both visible text and structured page metadata.
cards.explanation: Accurate, complete, and machine-readable disclosures allow both human shoppers and AI agents to evaluate offers fairly.
